title: C quiz: cumulative conceptual and code-reading assessment
learningObjectives: Recall and explain core C rules for expressions, types, arrays, pointers, functions, structures, files and dynamic storage.
Trace short C programs by tracking object values, pointer targets, control flow, function calls and observable output.
Distinguish defined behaviour from undefined behaviour, implementation-defined choices and assumptions that a program must state.
Evaluate input conversion, array bounds, pointer validity, resource ownership and arithmetic checks in realistic code fragments.
Apply a balanced assessment blueprint that samples foundational, intermediate and advanced course outcomes without over-weighting one topic.
Use answer explanations and misconception-focused feedback to plan targeted revision rather than memorising answer letters.

understand.concept:
A cumulative C quiz checks whether a learner can connect concepts from across the course, not merely repeat isolated definitions. A balanced assessment samples language foundations, types and expressions, control flow, arrays and strings, pointers and functions, structures and files, dynamic memory, standard-library use, algorithms, debugging and professional safety. Questions should measure both conceptual understanding and the ability to trace or review code.

A useful quiz blueprint maps every question to a learning outcome and a topic family before writing the question. Distribute questions across the course rather than allowing familiar topics to dominate. Include several cognitive levels: recall a rule; explain why it applies; trace a short fragment; diagnose a defect; and choose a safe design under stated constraints. Difficulty should come from reasoning, not obscure trivia or deliberately confusing wording.

Code-reading questions must be fully specified. State the relevant C version and assumptions when they affect the answer. Do not ask learners to predict output from a fragment that has undefined behaviour and then pretend there is one guaranteed output. Instead ask them to identify the undefined operation or explain why no portable output can be promised. Likewise, distinguish implementation-defined behaviour (the implementation documents its choice) from unspecified behaviour (one of several permitted outcomes without a requirement to document which one).

A strong multiple-choice item has one best answer, a focused prompt, plausible distractors based on common misconceptions, and an explanation that teaches the governing rule. Avoid “all of the above,” trick wording, accidental clues from option length and distractors that are obviously unrelated. Distractors should be wrong for a reason that can be explained. If multiple answers are defensible under the stated assumptions, revise the question rather than penalising the learner.

Use the quiz diagnostically. A missed question should point to a concept to revisit: array bounds, integer conversions, pointer lifetime, stream error handling, allocation ownership or algorithm preconditions. Feedback should explain why the selected answer is incorrect and what evidence or rule leads to the correct answer. A score is a snapshot of performance on this sample, not proof of complete mastery.
understand.whyItMatters: C programmers need to combine rules across language features. A cumulative assessment reveals gaps that isolated chapter quizzes can miss and gives learners a practical revision path before projects, interviews or professional code review.
understand.analogy: A cumulative quiz is like a systems check: each subsystem is sampled, then the results show where further inspection is needed.
understand.analogyLimit: A quiz samples performance and cannot prove that every program a learner writes is correct or that every course outcome has been mastered.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Blueprint and coverage balance

For a full course quiz, create a coverage matrix before writing questions. One reasonable 30-item blueprint is:

| Topic family | Suggested items | What to measure |
|---|---:|---|
| Foundations, compilation and types | 4 | declarations, conversions, format contracts, build stages |
| Operators and control flow | 3 | precedence, short-circuiting, loop tracing |
| Arrays, strings and input | 4 | bounds, terminators, conversion and truncation |
| Pointers and functions | 5 | lifetime, parameter contracts, const and return values |
| Structures, files and dynamic memory | 5 | representation, stream errors, ownership and realloc |
| Library, algorithms and debugging | 5 | API preconditions, complexity, diagnostics and tests |
| Standards and secure engineering | 4 | behaviour categories, overflow, portability and input trust |

The 30-item distribution is a blueprint, not a claim that this lesson contains 30 scored questions. The five lesson assessment questions below are a compact sample drawn from different course areas. A production quiz can select a larger item bank while preserving the same coverage rules.

## 2. Cognitive-level balance

A useful 30-item quiz might contain 6 recall questions, 8 explanation questions, 8 code-tracing questions, 4 defect-diagnosis questions and 4 design/application questions. Keep code fragments short enough that the intended concept is visible. For tracing questions, provide all declarations and relevant initial values. For output questions, specify the standard and avoid undefined behaviour unless identifying it is the point.

## 3. Difficulty and scoring

Tag items as introductory, intermediate or advanced. A balanced 30-item assessment might contain 9 introductory, 15 intermediate and 6 advanced questions. Use one point per item for a simple diagnostic score, but do not equate a percentage with complete mastery. A suggested review guide is: below 60% — revisit the relevant lessons and retry a shorter diagnostic; 60–79% — review missed concepts and complete targeted practice; 80–89% — attempt mixed code-reading and boundary exercises; 90% or above — attempt integrated challenges and explain the reasoning without notes. These are study suggestions, not validated certification cut-offs.

## 4. How to answer code-reading questions

Read declarations first, then determine each object's type, lifetime and initial value. Trace statements in execution order. For pointers, record the object each pointer designates and whether that object is still alive. For arrays, write the valid index interval before tracing an access. For integer expressions, apply promotions and conversions before evaluating. For library calls, check the function's preconditions and return value. Finally, ask whether the result is defined by the selected C standard or depends on implementation choices.

## 5. Worked example A: trace a pointer update and an array aggregation

The first example updates a caller-owned integer through a pointer, then passes an array and its explicit count to a function. Trace the function call and every loop iteration. The output is `score=10 total=11`. The array parameter does not carry the element count; the caller supplies it separately. The sum is accumulated in `long long` and the output parameter is written only after success.

## 6. Worked example B: validate and summarize structured records

The second example combines a structure, an enum status, an array, pointer-based function parameters, validation, a loop and a report. The function distinguishes invalid input, an empty collection and a completed report. The caller owns the records; the function does not allocate or retain them. The expected output is `passed=2 highest=88 total=209 average=69.67`.

## 7. Use feedback to choose revision work

Group missed items by concept rather than by question number. If several misses involve conversion, revisit integer ranges and checked parsing. If misses involve arrays and pointers, practise pointer/count contracts and object lifetime. If misses involve files or allocation, review stream status, ownership and cleanup. After revision, use a new set of questions or a fresh code trace; repeating the same answer pattern can measure memory of the quiz rather than understanding.

## 8. Assessment integrity checklist

- Each item maps to an explicit course outcome and topic family.
- The prompt states every assumption needed for one defensible answer.
- Code fragments have no accidental undefined behaviour unless that is being assessed.
- Distractors reflect real misconceptions and have explanatory feedback.
- Difficulty and cognitive level are tagged separately.
- The quiz covers the whole course proportionately and includes applied reasoning.
- Score bands are labelled as revision guidance, not certification.
- Learners can revisit the relevant lesson and attempt a fresh question set.

examples.title: Trace pointer mutation and array traversal
examples.explanation: `add_to_value` receives the address of `score`, checks the pointer and integer bounds, and adds three, changing the caller's value from 7 to 10. `sum_values` receives the array and its count, then accumulates 4 + (-2) + 9 + 0 in a `long long`. Expected output: `score=10 total=11`.

examples.title: Trace a validated structure summary and enum status
examples.explanation: `make_report` rejects a null output pointer or a null array with a nonzero count, returns a distinct empty status for zero records, and validates each learner's name and mark before updating a local report. It copies the completed report to the caller only after all records are valid. Expected output: `passed=2 highest=88 total=209 average=69.67`.

practise.guidedTask: Create a 10-question mini-quiz covering types, control flow, arrays, pointers, functions, structures, files, dynamic memory, algorithms and debugging. For every question, record its topic, cognitive level, difficulty, correct answer, misconception behind each distractor and a short explanation. Review the quiz for ambiguity before giving it to another learner.
practise.independentTask: Build a 30-item cumulative quiz using the coverage blueprint in this lesson. Include recall, explanation, code tracing, defect diagnosis and design/application items. State the C standard and assumptions for every code fragment. Include a separate answer key with explanations, tag each item by topic and difficulty, and write a revision recommendation for each topic family. Do not use undefined-behaviour fragments as ordinary output-prediction questions.
hints: Map questions to course outcomes first; write the quiz only after checking that every major topic family is represented.
For a code trace, list object values and pointer targets after each relevant statement instead of guessing the final output.
Check the selected C version, integer conversions, pointer lifetime and library preconditions before choosing an answer.
If a code fragment has undefined behaviour, ask learners to identify the defect; do not claim that it has one guaranteed output.
Write distractors from plausible misconceptions, then explain the precise rule that makes each one incorrect.
Use missed-question patterns to assign targeted revision and a fresh follow-up task rather than treating the score as a complete measure of mastery.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a C array parameter such as `int values[]` is correct?
options: The parameter is adjusted to a pointer parameter; the element count is not carried with it.
The parameter always contains the full array length.
The parameter is copied into a new array.
questions.answer: The parameter is adjusted to a pointer parameter; the element count is not carried with it.
questions.explanation: The array bound is not transmitted automatically with an adjusted pointer; pass a separate count.

questions.prompt: What does `sizeof values / sizeof values[0]` calculate when `values` is an actual array in the same scope?
options: The number of elements in that array.
The number of bytes in the first element.
The number of elements in any function parameter named values.
questions.answer: The number of elements in that array.
questions.explanation: Within the scope of a real array, sizeof the array divided by sizeof one element gives its element count. This does not work for an adjusted function parameter.

questions.prompt: Which operation is valid for a pointer to an element within an array?
options: Move it within the same array, including one past the last element for comparison, but do not dereference one-past.
Add any integer and dereference the result.
Subtract pointers that refer to unrelated objects.
questions.answer: Move it within the same array, including one past the last element for comparison, but do not dereference one-past.
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic is defined only within one array object or one past it; a one-past pointer may not be dereferenced.

questions.prompt: What is the key requirement before dereferencing a pointer parameter?
options: It must point to a live object of the appropriate type with valid access rights.
It must have been created with malloc.
It must have a nonzero numeric address representation.
questions.answer: It must point to a live object of the appropriate type with valid access rights.
questions.explanation: A pointer must designate a live, suitably typed object and the operation must be permitted by its qualifiers and lifetime.

questions.prompt: What is the result of integer division `-7 / 3` in C99 and later?
options: -2, with the fractional part discarded toward zero.
-3, rounded toward negative infinity.
-2.333..., because division always produces floating point.
questions.answer: -2, with the fractional part discarded toward zero.
questions.explanation: Since C99, integer division truncates toward zero, so -7 / 3 is -2.

questions.prompt: Which statement about signed integer overflow is correct?
options: It is undefined behaviour; check bounds before performing the operation.
It is guaranteed to wrap to the minimum value.
It is implementation-defined for every signed integer type.
questions.answer: It is undefined behaviour; check bounds before performing the operation.
questions.explanation: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour. Validate operands against the type limits before evaluating the operation.

questions.prompt: Why should `fgets`-based input be checked for truncation when the input contract limits line length?
options: A buffer may contain only a prefix of an overlong line, so the program must detect or drain/reject the remainder.
fgets automatically enlarges the destination array.
fgets always removes every whitespace character.
questions.answer: A buffer may contain only a prefix of an overlong line, so the program must detect or drain/reject the remainder.
questions.explanation: fgets stores at most capacity minus one characters. A truncated line must not be mistaken for a complete valid line.

questions.prompt: What must be checked after calling `strtol` for strict numeric input?
options: Whether digits were consumed, range errors, destination-type range and any disallowed trailing characters.
Only whether the returned value is nonzero.
Whether the input string contains a decimal point.
questions.answer: Whether digits were consumed, range errors, destination-type range and any disallowed trailing characters.
questions.explanation: strtol can accept a numeric prefix. A strict parser checks conversion, ERANGE, destination range and the remaining characters.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `const int *p` is correct?
options: The object cannot be modified through `p`, though it may be modifiable through another permitted access path.
The pointer itself cannot be changed to point elsewhere.
The pointed-to object must have static storage duration.
questions.answer: The object cannot be modified through `p`, though it may be modifiable through another permitted access path.
questions.explanation: const qualifies the pointed-to type, not the pointer object itself.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `realloc` is safest when resizing may fail?
options: Store the result in a temporary pointer and update the owning pointer only on success.
Assign directly to the only owning pointer and assume failure preserves it.
Call free on the original pointer before realloc.
questions.answer: Store the result in a temporary pointer and update the owning pointer only on success.
questions.explanation: On realloc failure, the original allocation remains valid. A temporary preserves the only owning pointer.

questions.prompt: What does `fopen` returning a null pointer indicate?
options: The requested stream could not be opened; inspect the failure and do not use it as a valid stream.
The file is empty but successfully opened.
The stream is positioned at end-of-file.
questions.answer: The requested stream could not be opened; inspect the failure and do not use it as a valid stream.
questions.explanation: An unsuccessful fopen returns a null pointer; stream operations require a successfully opened stream.

questions.prompt: Which statement about structure assignment is correct?
options: Assignment copies the structure value, including array members as part of the structure value.
Assignment compares all members and returns a Boolean.
Assignment duplicates dynamically allocated objects referenced by pointer members.
questions.answer: Assignment copies the structure value, including array members as part of the structure value.
questions.explanation: Structure assignment copies member values. Pointer members are copied as pointer values; separately allocated targets are not cloned.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a function prototype visible before a call?
options: It declares the function's type so the call can be checked and interpreted correctly.
It allocates storage for every local variable in the function.
It forces the compiler to inline the function.
questions.answer: It declares the function's type so the call can be checked and interpreted correctly.
questions.explanation: A visible declaration supplies the function type needed for correct call checking.

options: Free only a pointer returned by a compatible allocation function that has not already been freed; do not use the allocation afterward.
Free may be called repeatedly on the same pointer.
Free releases automatic local arrays.
questions.answer: Free only a pointer returned by a compatible allocation function that has not already been freed; do not use the allocation afterward.
questions.explanation: free has strict allocation and lifetime requirements; double-free and use-after-free are undefined behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which combination gives stronger evidence that a C program is correct and robust?
options: Reason from contracts, compile with warnings, run boundary tests and use suitable analysis/sanitizers.
Run one sample once and ignore compiler warnings.
Use only the compiler that happened to build the program.
questions.answer: Reason from contracts, compile with warnings, run boundary tests and use suitable analysis/sanitizers.
questions.explanation: Multiple complementary checks reveal different classes of defects; none alone proves correctness.
